rv.q: Too big to be contained within the regular loop of the auditorium, even when the director uses the full height of the in-the-round space, sending her actors up ladders and getting them to pop out from the upper level. More than that, before the show and in the interval, her production spills into the wider building.
Selina Cartmell’s revival of Jim Cartwright’s 40-year-old debut, starring Lucy Beaumont, Johnny Vegas and Shobna Gulati, zooms in on the tragedy of this bleakly poetic play
At 50, the Royal Exchange proves it can still stage that howl with thrilling immediacy.

But there is no denying that this is a relentlessly bleak window into the midst of Thatcher's Britain, a time that was hard for a lot of people at the lower end of the social scale but which, from my memory, had a lot more lighter moments than are seen in this play.
This revival is bold, atmospheric, and unapologetically theatrical, the kind of work that reminds audiences why live performance matters.

cn.t: Critics praise Cartmell's bold, immersive revival of Cartwright's working-class portrait, with standout performances and theatrical ambition transforming the Royal Exchange into a vivid 1980s estate, though the episodic structure occasionally falters.
